1a5e95ea29520134aa86161df09979c2e217d020.summary: A 2017 blog post by Brian Reitz that builds a PowerShell proof of concept, using the PSReflect tool, to write a Windows registry Run key value whose name starts with a null character. The post links this persistence trick to Kovter malware. It says Regedit and similar tools fail to show the value, while the Sysinternals Autoruns tool still does. The author presents it to help defenders test detection of such registry persistence.

1acc2a8d239c6e3174bbec8dcce33dc1175d6f02.summary: This page is a promotional landing page for a Qualys Threat Research Team report on Quasar RAT, an open-source remote access trojan. It invites readers to download the full report without registration. The page gives only a short overview and asks readers to download the rest, so it is treated as a marketing piece and the fact lists are left empty.

1aa5a21d68cedb2cffb923a011be8e5cd7b1bb64.summary: eSentire's Threat Response Unit stopped an intrusion at a product safety testing organization in late July, before any ransomware was deployed. Initial access was through a vulnerable SharePoint server, followed by Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz use and attempts to disable endpoint monitoring. The Hello Ransomware group's tactics resemble those of Chinese espionage groups such as Emissary Panda (APT27) and UNC215. The report stresses that attribution is uncertain: the overlap could be a false flag, and the group's link to espionage or the Chinese state is unproven.

hedges: The report says the attack could be part of a false flag campaign.
TRU has no strong evidence connecting Chinese espionage groups and Hello Ransomware, only an overlap in techniques and tools.
Unit 42 notes similarities to Emissary Panda campaigns but hesitates to draw conclusions, as no strong pivot points connect them.
FireEye says it had not observed Emissary Panda activity since 2015, challenging the notion that it was behind recent ransomware attacks.
The report says a non-Chinese group could intentionally adopt Chinese tactics to mislead analysis.
The report says it is impossible to tell which implementation of Mimikatz was used.
Per FireEye analysis, the 2019 SharePoint campaigns attributed to Emissary Panda by Palo Alto may instead be run by UNC215, with uncertain ties to Emissary Panda.
